title-group.article-title: Empirical Studies of the Aviris Hyperspectral Data Signatures of Different Earth Terrains

institution-wrap.institution: Department of Earth, Environmental, and Geospatial Science

abstract.p: Hyperspectral images and optical signatures acquired by NASA's Airborne Visible/Infrared Imaging Spectrometer (AVIRIS) from multiple locations are examined. The spectral responses obtained are used to promote the development of physics-based models for these signatures with future application in improvements in hyperspectral sensing.

sec.label: I.
sec.title: Introduction
sec.p:
Hyperspectral visible/infrared sensors capture images using hundreds of narrow continuous spectral bands that span a wide portion of the optical and infrared spectrum. Such data provide a better spectral characterization of objects that can be used to improve the sensing of various material and/or scene properties [1]. A variety of hyperspectral systems have been or are currently available from satellite and aerial vehicle platforms, as summarized in Table I. Table I. List of recent satellite or airborne missions employing hyperspectral imaging sensors

AVIRISClassic Active 20 224 10 400-2500 [3]
AVIRISNG Active 5 425 5 380-2510 [4]
PRISMA Active 30 239 12 400-2505 [5]
EnMAP Active 30 246 6.5, 10 420-2450 [6]
Tanager Active 30 400 5 420-2500 [7]
Pixxel Active 10 250 nan 450-900 [8]
HysPIRI Planned 60 242 10,90 380-2500, 3000-12000 [9]

Data from NASA's Airborne Visible/Infrared Imaging Spectrometer (AVIRIS) system have been used in various applications, including mapping vegetation health, geology, soil analysis, and monitoring environmental hazards, establishing it as a valuable resource for hyperspectral imaging [10]. AVIRIS has flown extensively across North America, Europe, and in portions of South America to detect and monitor Earth's surface and atmospheric elements [11]. Its successor, AVIRIS-NG, has expanded these efforts with extensive investigations in locations like Alaska and Canada, particularly through the Arctic-Boreal Vulnerability Experiment (ABoVE) [12].

Hyperspectral remote sensing typically maps and monitors changes in Earth's terrain using statistical and empirical models focused on bio-geophysical variables (vegetation, topography, active layer thickness, etc.). The models applied in this process typically result from data-oriented approaches with only limited regard for the underlying physical mechanisms causing the observed reflectance signatures. A physics-based modeling approach can be valuable for improving hyperspectral sensing, but often can be difficult due to the many factors that can impact the reflection, scattering, and propagation of optical and infrared signals. A combination of physics-based approaches that leverage insights from empirical studies is therefore well motivated. Here we report an analysis of example images from multiple locations with the objective of understanding how we may use empirical investigations to support ongoing development of a physics-based forward model.

sec.label: II.
sec.title: Example Cases
sec.p: Four example images acquired from AVIRIS flights over Fairbanks, Alaska, USA; Colville Forest, Washington, USA; Greenland; and the Norwegian Sea are examined. All of the images were obtained from the AVIRIS data portal [13], with each depicting a distinct environmental scenario. It should be noted that the analysis spans the 400 nm to 2500 nm range of observations available, which includes visible, near-infrared (NIR), and short-wave infrared (SWIR) wavelengths. Because hyperspectral data is susceptible to atmospheric water vapor and CO2 absorption around 1400, 1900, and 2000 nm [14], data from wavelengths 1300-1500 nm and 1800-2050 nm is discarded in the following discussion.

sec.label: A.
sec.title: Fairbanks, Alaska, USA
sec.p: The left portion of Fig. 1 is an RGB composite image of an area of Fairbanks, Alaska taken on Aug 01, 2023, with corresponding spectral data on the right. The reflectance values are first averaged over three samples along the central image line and then normalized across the entire spectrum for each location coordinate. The image shows vegetation with thin clouds and their associated shadows. For pixels with vegetation and no clouds, the corresponding response in the visible spectrum between 400 and 700 nm is dominated by light absorption of leaf pigments [15] and by similar strong leaf pigment and cellulose reflections in the 700 nm-1300 nm region. The higher wavelength region (1500 nm-2500 nm) is dominated by soil and leaf water absorption, resulting in reduced reflected radiation in this portion of the spectrum. Fig. 1 also shows that clouds produce a strong reflectance response at wavelengths less than 1300 nm.

sec.label: B.
sec.title: Colville Forest, Washington, USA
sec.p:
Fig. 2 presents an image with a fire event in the Colville forest taken on September 8, 2022. Pixels with non-burning vegetation and no clouds or smoke exhibit values similar to those in Fig. 1. The forest fire appears in the center of the RGB composite image on the left side of Fig. 2. The normalized reflectance curve reveals high values in the SWIR range (1500-2500 nm) for the associated pixels. The reflectance outcome for the smoke is quite similar to the cloud response seen in Fig. 1. The vegetated area has also been reduced and appears to be bare soil in the image.
Fig. 1.
Spectral data along a flight path in fairbanks, alaska: geospatial rgb composite image (left) and normalized reflectance profile by location (right).
Fig. 2.
Spectral data along a flight path in colville forest, washington: geospatial rgb composite image (left) and normalized reflectance profile by location (right).

sec.label: C.
sec.title: Norwegian Sea
sec.p:
The image taken in the Norwegian Sea on May 16, 2021 consists of cloud covered sea water. The spectral response is shown in Fig. 3 and indicates that clouds completely obscure the image. As a result, high reflectance values are observed in the 400 nm-1300 nm range, which is typical of a white object. Because of the cloud's inconsistencies, the reflectance varies slightly as the location changes.
Fig. 3.
Spectral data along a flight path in the norwegian sea: geospatial rgb composite image (left) and normalized reflectance profile by location (right).
Fig. 4.
Spectral data along a flight path in greenland: geospatial rgb composite image (left) and normalized reflectance profile by location (right).

sec.label: D.
sec.title: Greenland
sec.p: The final image of a snowy area of Greenland (taken on September 4, 2019) appears completely white. As a result, a near-spatially constant response is seen in Fig. 4. The response is somewhat similar to that of the cloud-covered sea water in Fig. 3.

To compare the reflective response from various geographic locations with wavelength, different pixels from these four images were chosen. The reflectance values for each spectral band were first averaged over a 10 -pixel radius around the intended point to eliminate the effect of noise and outliers. The reflectance curves of these pixels of different environments were then plotted against wavelength in Fig. 5. The regions represent various locations, including a vegetated area in Fairbanks; a fireaffected region, a vegetated area, and a bare soil area in the Colville Forest; a snowy site in Greenland; and cloud-covered seawater in the Norwegian Sea. The figure shows that vegetation from Fairbanks retains the expected shape of low reflectance in the visible spectrum and high reflectance in the NIR region. Moreover, a similar response is observed from the vegetated area in the Colville forest. Another pixel taken from a burned area has a reflectance value that gradually increases from visible to NIR to SWIR. The response coincides with other reported studies [16], [17]. The other pixel from this forest was taken in an area with little vegetation and resembles bare soil. The flat response of reflectance across the entire spectrum is indicative of dry soil [15]. The pixel containing a snowy zone has a high reflective value in the visible spectrum but gradually decreases until the end of the NIR band. The cloud-covered sea water responds similarly to the snow, but with a lower value in the visible spectrum due to the uneven clouds. However, the values in the SWIR are higher than those in other pixels due to the presence of water droplets.
Fig. 5.
Reflectance values of different locations against wavelengths.

sec.label: III.
sec.title: Spectral Index Calculations
sec.p:
We computed the three indices for the first two images under investigation along the track for the center pixels using (1), (2), and (4). Fig. 6 illustrates these results for Fairbanks. High values of NDVI (around 0.8) can be observed except for the dips that occur when clouds are present. The NDWI is close to zero, and the NDSI is less than zero much of the track. However, greater than zero values can be observed for NDSI when the cloud is very thick.
Fig. 6.
NDVI, ndwi, and ndsi along central line (fairbanks, alaska)

Similarly, Fig. 7 shows the indices for the Colville forest. Again, high values of NDVI are typically obtained that decrease in smoke-obscured or burned areas. The NDWI and NDSI follow trends similar to those in Fig. 6, while NDSI>0 appears to be responsive to the presence of smoke.
Fig. 7.
NDVI, ndwi, and ndsi along central line (colville forest, washington)

Fig. 8 and Fig. 9 depict the indices for cloud-covered seawater from the Norwegian Sea and the snowy region from Greenland, respectively. In these scenarios, (3) was used instead of (2) to compute the NDWI. Fig. 8 shows higher NDSI values than NDWI due to the image's dense cloud coverage. The NDVI and NDWI are closer to 0. On the other hand, the NDSI index is able to capture the snowy condition in Fig. 9. The NDSI values are higher, as expected, while the NDVI values are closer to 0. The presence of water molecules causes NDWI values to be slightly greater than 0. The NDSI values in Fig. 9 are greater than those in Fig. 8, indicating that the snowy zones can be distinguished correctly from the cloud.
Fig. 8.
NDVI, ndwi, and ndsi along central line (cloud-covered norwegian sea)
Fig. 9.
NDVI, ndwi, and ndsi along central line (greenland)

sec.label: IV.
sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: The examples presented here demonstrate some of the properties of hyperspectral data under different environmental conditions. Existing data-driven approaches are available to exploit such datasets in sensing applications. Our ongoing work seeks to use the insights obtained from these analyses to promote the development of a physics-based approach to support continuing improvements in Earth remote sensing.
